lesson_title: Gate, Floor, Office, Generator: The Cell as a Spaza Shop
hook_text: You are made of about 30 trillion tiny spaza shops. Each one has a gate, a floor, an office and a generator.
clip_script: Every cell in your body is a tiny spaza shop. Four parts. The security gate is the cell membrane: thin, but it chooses what comes in and what goes out. Oxygen and glucose in, carbon dioxide out, trouble stays outside. Selectively permeable. The shop floor is the cytoplasm: mostly water, and it is where every chemical reaction of the cell happens. The back office is the nucleus, and the recipe book on its shelf is DNA, 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, every instruction for running the shop. No book, no new stock, no repairs. That is why the nucleus controls the cell. And the generator in the corner is the mitochondrion. Glucose plus oxygen in, energy out. A busy muscle cell has thousands of them; a lazy skin cell has a few. Now the size: a cheek cell is 60 micrometres, five times smaller than a grain of salt. Stack a 10 times eyepiece on a 40 times objective, 400 times, add a drop of methylene blue, and that dark office in the middle appears.
visual_style: A cartoon spaza shop morphs into a cheek cell: the gate becomes the membrane outline, the floor the pale cytoplasm, the office a dark nucleus, the generator a sausage-shaped mitochondrion; a grain of salt shrinks to a cell, then a microscope zooms in.
pacing: Four fast beats for the four parts, a pause on 'controls the cell', then a zoom-in finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and label any cell drawing for full marks.
